newsitem.title: USA: IMF praises Irish economy, sees overheating risk.
newsitem.headline: IMF praises Irish economy, sees overheating risk.

text.p: Ireland can sustain growth above the EU average in the medium term, but must be ready to tighten policy if the economy starts to overheat, the International Monetary Fund said on Friday.

A statement released after the IMF reviewed the Irish economy said Ireland's "impressive economic performance" had been marked by rapid growth and job creation, falling unemployment and low inflation.
"Ireland had made welcome progress in raising living standards and appeared well positioned to be among the first members of the euro area," the IMF said.
The IMF said developments in Ireland's labour market and productivity indicated that the country could sustain growth well above the EU average in the medium term. But it added:

"(IMF) directors were of the view that continued growth at the pace of the past few years carried risks of overheating. They encouraged the authorities to be vigilant for signs of emerging strains, with particular attention to the tightening labour and housing markets.
"They therefore welcomed the authorities' readiness to tighten macro-economic policies as needed."

The IMF projected Irish GDP growth of 6.5 percent, down from 6.9 percent in 1996. Consumer prices would rise 1.7 percent after 1.6 percent in 1996, while unemployment would fall to 10.3 percent from 11.2 percent last year.
"Outward-oriented policies, financial discipline, wage moderation and significant EU assistance have yielded dramatic progress for the Irish economy over the past decade," it said.
"Since 1987 growth has averaged almost five percent per annum -- the fastest in the EU -- while inflation has been maintained consistently below the EU average."

The IMF said that the implementation of monetary policy in recent months had been complicated by the fact that the Irish pound was strong within the Exchange Rate Mechanism of the EU and that markets expected Irish interest rates to "converge downward" by the start of EMU.

"(Directors) agreed that, given the economy's robust growth, the central bank should not seek to hasten that convergence process and that the recent policy tightening had been appropriate," the statement said.
The IMF reviews the state of the economy of each member country once a year and the reviews are sometimes followed by a press notice.
